expectedText:
LLC MEMBER AND MANAGER FIDUCIARY DUTIES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Ventures, LLC · Jordan Lee

IDENTIFICATION
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee, a member or manager of Acme Ventures, LLC, a California limited liability company, and Casey Alex, another member of that limited liability company. It addresses the fiduciary duties that California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act assigns to a member or manager, how those duties are reallocated in a manager-managed limited liability company, and the extent to which the limited liability company's own operating agreement may modify those duties.

THE TWO STATUTORY FIDUCIARY DUTIES IN A MEMBER-MANAGED LLC
California's limited liability company statute states that a member's fiduciary duties to a member-managed limited liability company and to the other members consist of exactly two duties — a duty of loyalty and a duty of care — and that each of those duties is defined and limited by a separate subdivision of the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The fiduciary duties that a member owes to a member-managed limited liability company and the other members of the limited liability company are the duties of loyalty and care under subdivisions (b) and (c)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the two fiduciary duties a member owes in a member-managed LLC (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(a). It does not state the content of either duty, which companion clauses of this document address separately by quoting subdivisions (b) and (c). It applies by its own terms to a member-managed limited liability company; a companion clause of this document (id: llcduty_manager_managed_reallocation, citing § 17704.09(f)) addresses how these same duties are reallocated to the manager or managers, and away from the members, in a manager-managed limited liability company. No case law was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search for California opinions citing this subdivision by name returned no on-point results within the scope of this research.

DUTY OF LOYALTY: ACCOUNTING FOR PROPERTY, PROFIT, AND LLC OPPORTUNITIES
The first component of the statutory duty of loyalty is an accounting duty: a member subject to the duty must account to the limited liability company, and hold as trustee for it, any property, profit, or benefit the member derives in the conduct or winding up of the limited liability company's activities, or derives from using limited liability company property — and the statute specifically includes within this duty the appropriation of a limited liability company opportunity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "To account to the limited liability company and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the member in the conduct and winding up of the activities of a limited liability company or derived from a use by the member of a limited liability company property, including the appropriation of a limited liability company opportunity."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, accounting for property, profit, or benefit including appropriation of an LLC opportunity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(b)(1). It does not define what makes an opportunity a "limited liability company opportunity" for purposes of the appropriation rule, a line-drawing question the statute leaves to case-by-case application. It does not address the operating agreement's power to narrow this duty, which a separate clause of this document addresses (id: llcduty_agreement_loyalty_carveout, citing Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(14)). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

DUTY OF LOYALTY: REFRAINING FROM ADVERSE-INTEREST DEALING
The second component of the statutory duty of loyalty requires a member subject to the duty to refrain from dealing with the limited liability company, in the conduct or winding up of its activities, as or on behalf of a person whose interest is adverse to the limited liability company's own interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "To refrain from dealing with the limited liability company in the conduct or winding up of the activities of the limited liability company as or on behalf of a person having an interest adverse to the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, refraining from adverse-interest dealing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(b)(2). It does not define what makes an interest "adverse," nor does it address whether or how the operating agreement's ratification mechanism (a separate clause of this document, id: llcduty_agreement_loyalty_carveout, citing § 17701.10(c)(14)(B)) can authorize a specific adverse-interest transaction after full disclosure. It does not address remedies for a violation of this component. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

DUTY OF LOYALTY: REFRAINING FROM COMPETING WITH THE LLC
The third component of the statutory duty of loyalty requires a member subject to the duty to refrain from competing with the limited liability company in the conduct or winding up of its activities.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "To refrain from competing with the limited liability company in the conduct or winding up of the activities of the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, refraining from competing with the limited liability company (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(b)(3). It does not define what constitutes "competing" with the limited liability company, and does not address whether the operating agreement can carve out specific competitive activities in advance, a mechanism a separate clause of this document addresses generally (id: llcduty_agreement_loyalty_carveout). It does not address any duty that might continue, or end, after a member dissociates. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

DUTY OF CARE: A GROSS-NEGLIGENCE STANDARD
The statutory duty of care owed by a member subject to the duty, to the limited liability company and the other members, in the conduct and winding up of the limited liability company's activities, is limited to refraining from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law. Ordinary negligence, standing alone, is not stated as a basis for a duty-of-care violation under this subdivision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A member’s duty of care to a limited liability company and the other members in the conduct and winding up of the activities of the limited liability company is limited to refraining from engaging in grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the duty-of-care standard for a member (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(c). It does not define "grossly negligent," "reckless," or "knowing violation of law" beyond the statute's own words, and it does not address the operating agreement's power to reduce this standard further, which is limited by a separate provision (a companion clause of this document, id: llcduty_agreement_care_carveout, citing Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(15), which prohibits an "unreasonable" reduction but does not itself define that line). No case law construing this specific subdivision was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search for California opinions applying this gross-negligence standard to an LLC member or manager returned no on-point results within the scope of this research.

THE OBLIGATION OF GOOD FAITH AND FAIR DEALING, AND THE SELF-INTEREST CARVE-OUT
Beyond the two named fiduciary duties, the statute separately requires a member to discharge duties to the limited liability company and the other members, and to exercise any rights, consistently with an obligation of good faith and fair dealing. The statute then adds a limiting principle: a member does not violate a duty or obligation merely because the member's conduct furthers the member's own interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A member shall discharge the duties to a limited liability company and the other members under this title or under the operating agreement and exercise any rights consistent with the obligation of good faith and fair dealing."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the good faith and fair dealing obligation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  "A member does not violate a duty or obligation under this article or under the operating agreement merely because the member’s conduct furthers the member’s own interest."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, self-interested conduct alone is not a violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(d) and (e). It does not define "good faith and fair dealing" beyond the statute's own words, and it does not resolve how the self-interest carve-out in subdivision (e) interacts with the specific duty-of-loyalty prohibitions in subdivision (b) — for example, whether conduct that both furthers the member's own interest and independently breaches subdivision (b)(2)'s adverse-interest rule is excused by subdivision (e) or still prohibited by subdivision (b). The statute's text does not itself resolve that interaction. Subdivision (d)'s good-faith obligation applies to both members and managers, while subdivision (e)'s self-interest carve-out applies only as reallocated by subdivision (f), addressed in a separate clause of this document (id: llcduty_manager_managed_reallocation). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

HOW THESE DUTIES SHIFT IN A MANAGER-MANAGED LLC
In a manager-managed limited liability company, the statute reallocates the duties described elsewhere in this document. The duty-source rule, the three components of the duty of loyalty, and the self-interest carve-out apply to the manager or managers and not to the members. The good-faith-and-fair-dealing obligation, by contrast, applies to both members and managers. And except as otherwise provided, a member does not have any fiduciary duty to the limited liability company, or to any other member, solely by reason of being a member.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (e) apply to the manager or managers and not the members."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duties shift to the manager in a manager-managed LLC (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  "Subdivision (d) applies to the members and managers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, good faith and fair dealing applies to both members and managers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  "Except as otherwise provided, a member does not have any fiduciary duty to the limited liability company or to any other member solely by reason of being a member."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member has no fiduciary duty solely by reason of being a member (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(f)(1)-(3). It does not identify the other provisions of law that might supply an exception to paragraph (3)'s "except as otherwise provided" language, a question the statute leaves to other sections of this title or to the operating agreement. It does not address whether a member of a manager-managed limited liability company who is also a manager owes duties in both capacities, a combination the statute's text does not directly address in this subdivision. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

WHAT THE OPERATING AGREEMENT MAY NOT DO: A GENERAL BAR ON ELIMINATING FIDUCIARY DUTY
California's limited liability company statute lists specific things an operating agreement is not permitted to do, and one of them, in general terms, is eliminating the duty of loyalty, the duty of care, or any other fiduciary duty. This general bar is itself made subject to two narrower carve-outs elsewhere in the same subdivision, addressed separately in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Subject to paragraphs (14) and (15) of this subdivision and subdivisions (d) to (g), inclusive, eliminate the duty of loyalty, the duty of care, or any other fiduciary duty."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the operating agreement may not eliminate fiduciary duty generally (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(4). It does not state the content of the two carve-outs it references — paragraph (14)'s duty-of-loyalty carve-outs and paragraph (15)'s duty-of-care limit — which separate clauses of this document address (id: llcduty_agreement_loyalty_carveout and id: llcduty_agreement_care_carveout). It does not address the four other subdivisions this paragraph is made "subject to" (subdivisions (d) through (g) of the same section), of which this document separately addresses subdivision (e)'s informed-consent requirement and subdivision (g)'s liability-limitation provision. It does not address the eleven other restrictions the same subdivision (c) places on what an operating agreement may vary that are unrelated to fiduciary duty (for example, the power to sue and be sued, or the requirements for dissolution). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

WHAT THE OPERATING AGREEMENT MAY DO INSTEAD: NARROW, BUT NOT ELIMINATE, THE DUTY OF LOYALTY
The statute separately confirms that an operating agreement may not eliminate the duty of loyalty described elsewhere in this document, but permits the operating agreement to do two narrower things instead: identify specific types or categories of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, so long as doing so is not manifestly unreasonable, and specify what number or percentage of members may authorize or ratify — after full disclosure of all material facts — a specific act or transaction that would otherwise violate the duty of loyalty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Eliminate the duty of loyalty under subdivision (b) of Section 17704.09, but the operating agreement may do any of the following:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the operating agreement may not eliminate the duty of loyalty, subject to two carve-outs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  "Identify specific types or categories of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, identifying non-violating categories of activity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  "Specify the number or percentage of members that may authorize or ratify, after full disclosure to all members of all material facts, a specific act or transaction that otherwise would violate the duty of loyalty."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, authorization or ratification after full disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(14), including its two lettered sub-provisions. It does not define "manifestly unreasonable," a standard the statute leaves undefined. It does not address subdivision (e)'s separate requirement that any modification of fiduciary duty be made in a written operating agreement with the members' informed consent, which a companion clause of this document addresses (id: llcduty_informed_consent_requirement). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

WHAT THE OPERATING AGREEMENT MAY NOT DO: UNREASONABLY REDUCE THE DUTY OF CARE
The same statutory list of restrictions also addresses the duty of care described elsewhere in this document. An operating agreement may not unreasonably reduce that duty of care.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Unreasonably reduce the duty of care under subdivision (c) of Section 17704.09."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, no unreasonable reduction of the duty of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(15). Unlike the loyalty restriction in paragraph (14), paragraph (15) permits some reduction of the duty of care — only an "unreasonable" reduction is barred — and the statute does not itself define the line between a reasonable and an unreasonable reduction. No case law was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search located no California opinion applying this paragraph to a specific operating agreement provision.

WHAT THE OPERATING AGREEMENT MAY NOT DO: ELIMINATE GOOD FAITH AND FAIR DEALING
The statute also bars an operating agreement from eliminating the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing described elsewhere in this document, though it permits the operating agreement to prescribe the standards by which performance of that obligation is measured, so long as those standards are not manifestly unreasonable as determined at the time they are prescribed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Subject to subdivisions (d) to (g), inclusive, eliminate the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing under subdivision (d) of Section 17704.09, but the operating agreement may prescribe the standards by which the performance of the obligation is to be measured, if the standards are not manifestly unreasonable as determined at the time the standards are prescribed."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, no elimination of the good faith and fair dealing obligation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(5). It does not define "manifestly unreasonable," a standard the statute leaves undefined, and it does not address the four subdivisions ((d) through (g)) this paragraph is made subject to. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

MODIFYING THESE DUTIES REQUIRES A WRITTEN OPERATING AGREEMENT AND INFORMED CONSENT
The statute imposes a separate procedural requirement on any modification of these fiduciary duties: the fiduciary duties of a manager, or of a member in a member-managed limited liability company, may only be modified in a written operating agreement with the members' informed consent. The statute specifically states that merely assenting to the operating agreement does not, by itself, constitute that informed consent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The fiduciary duties of a manager to a manager-managed limited liability company and to the members of the limited liability company and of a member to a member-managed limited liability company and to the members of such limited liability company shall only be modified in a written operating agreement with the informed consent of the members. Assenting to the operating agreement pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 17701.11 shall not constitute informed consent."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, modifying fiduciary duties requires a written operating agreement and informed consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(e). It does not define "informed consent" beyond stating what does not satisfy it, and it does not address what process would satisfy the requirement. It does not address subdivision (f), a related provision (not quoted in this document) under which an operating agreement that relieves one member of a responsibility and shifts it to other members may correspondingly adjust the fiduciary duty tied to that responsibility. No case law was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search for California opinions construing this informed-consent requirement returned no on-point results within the scope of this research.

THE OPERATING AGREEMENT'S POWER TO LIMIT MONEY-DAMAGES LIABILITY, AND ITS EXCEPTIONS
Separately from the duty-modification rules described elsewhere in this document, the statute permits an operating agreement to alter or eliminate the indemnification the statute otherwise makes available to a member or manager, and to eliminate or limit a member's or manager's liability to the limited liability company and the other members for money damages — but the statute excepts several categories of conduct from that liability limitation, including a breach of the duty of loyalty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The operating agreement may alter or eliminate the indemnification for a member or manager provided by subdivision (a) of Section 17704.08 and may eliminate or limit a member or manager’s liability to the limited liability company and members for money damages, except for the following:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the operating agreement may limit money-damages liability, subject to exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  "Breach of the duty of loyalty."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, breach of the duty of loyalty cannot be excused by such a provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(g), together with paragraph (1) of its list of exceptions (breach of the duty of loyalty). It does not quote the other four exceptions listed in paragraphs (2) through (5) of the same subdivision — a financial benefit the member or manager was not entitled to receive, a member's liability for excess distributions under Section 17704.06, intentional infliction of harm on the limited liability company or a member, and an intentional violation of criminal law — each of which independently bars a liability limitation for that category of conduct. It does not address the indemnification statute, Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.08(a), that this provision permits an operating agreement to alter. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

PREPARATION AND SIGNATURE BLOCK
This information sheet regarding the fiduciary duties of Jordan Lee as a member or manager of Acme Ventures, LLC was prepared by Jordan Lee.

Executed on September 9, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________
